# Fireball Brightness

**AJ Lapicola**

## Introduction

Many of us have seen flashes of light streak across the sky, only to vanish in seconds. What we often call "shoooting stars" are in fact, meators. Most meteors are faint, but some blaze so brightly that they’re called fireballs. They begin as small pieces of rock or metal traveling through space; when they plunge into Earth’s atmosphere, they heat the surrounding air and shed material, creating a brilliant glow. NASA’s CNEOS database collects reports of some of these events, offering a glimpse of a dramatic process that usually lasts only moments.

I’m curious about what these records can tell us about a fireball’s passage through the atmosphere. In particular, I want to explore whether altitude at peak brightness and entry speed are associated with how much energy a fireball radiates. Looking at these characteristics could help me better understand what more energetic fireballs have in common.

How are factors like altitude at peak brightness, entry speed, location, and others associated with the radiated energy of a fireball?

## Responsible Data Collection

I will collect the data through the official NASA/JPL CNEOS Fireball Data API and follow JPL’s [Fair Use Policy](https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/). As such, I will make only the requests needed for my project, send one request at a time, and save the results so I can reuse them rather than repeatedly requesting the same data. My script will include an application-specific User-Agent with its name, version, and contact information, and will handle errors by backing off before retrying. I will also check the API version in each response. The records describe fireball events and do not contain personal information.

## Data Collection

To collect the fireball records, I used Python’s `requests` library to send a GET request to NASA/JPL’s [CNEOS Fireball Data API](https://ssd-api.jpl.nasa.gov/doc/fireball.html). I included parameters requiring records to have location, altitude, and entry velocity components, and requested the velocity fields. After checking the response for HTTP errors, I converted its JSON content into a pandas DataFrame, using the API’s `fields` list as column names. I saved this initial version as a CSV file in `data/raw`, preserving a copy of the data before cleaning.

To prepare the data for analysis, I read the CSV back into pandas, converted the date column to datetime format, and converted the latitude, longitude, altitude, energy, impact energy, and velocity columns to numeric values. Someone following a similar process can adjust the API parameters, retrieve JSON records, and convert them into a structured dataset for exploration.

## EDA highlights: summary statistics, summary graphics, and/or information about final dataset (e.g., total sample size, counts of categorical variables, numerical summaries of numeric variables)
What are the most interesting findings of your EDA?
```{python}
#| include: false

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import seaborn as sns

#read in raw data
fireballs = pd.read_csv("data/raw/fireballs_raw.csv")

#convert data column to pandas date object
fireballs["date"] = pd.to_datetime(fireballs["date"], errors="coerce")

#convert numeric columns
numeric_columns = ["lat", "lon", "alt", "energy", "impact-e", "vx", "vy", "vz"]
for column in numeric_columns:
    if column in fireballs.columns:
        fireballs[column] = pd.to_numeric(fireballs[column], errors="coerce")

#create speed column by velocity components
fireballs["speed"] = np.sqrt(
    fireballs[["vx", "vy", "vz"]].pow(2).sum(axis=1, min_count=3)
)

fireballs.head()
```

### Summary Table
```{python}
#| echo: False

#variables of interest
eda_vars = ["energy", "alt", "speed"]

#summary statistics
summary = fireballs[eda_vars].agg(
    ["count", "median", "min", "max"]
).T

#generate summaries
summary["missing"] = fireballs[eda_vars].isna().sum()
summary["IQR"] = (
    fireballs[eda_vars].quantile(0.75)
    - fireballs[eda_vars].quantile(0.25)
)

#create dataframe and display info
summary = summary[["count", "missing", "median", "IQR", "min", "max"]]

print(f"Rows: {len(fireballs)}")
print(f"Columns: {len(fireballs.columns)}")

summary
```

### Radiated Energy Distribution
```{python}
#| echo: False

#use log scale for energy
bins = np.logspace(
    np.log10(fireballs["energy"].min()),
    np.log10(fireballs["energy"].max()),
    25,
)

#histogram to display overall energy distribution
sns.histplot(data=fireballs, x="energy", bins=bins, edgecolor="white")

plt.xscale("log")
plt.xlabel("Total radiated energy (10^10 joules, log scale)")
plt.ylabel("Number of fireballs")
plt.title("Distribution of Fireball Radiated Energy")
plt.show()
```

### Associations
```{python}
#| echo: False

#use log scale for energy
alt_data = fireballs[["alt", "energy"]].copy()
alt_data["log_energy"] = np.log10(alt_data["energy"])

#scatterplot with trendline to highlight relationship
sns.regplot(
    data=alt_data,
    x="alt",
    y="log_energy",
    ci=None,
    scatter_kws={"alpha": 0.6},
)

plt.xlabel("Altitude at peak brightness (km)")
plt.ylabel("log10 radiated energy (10^10 joules)")
plt.title("Altitude and Radiated Energy")
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: False

#use log scale for energy

plt.xlabel("Calculated entry speed (km/s)")
plt.ylabel("log10 radiated energy (10^10 joules)")
plt.title("Entry Speed and Radiated Energy")
plt.show()
```
